name: New Jersey
overview: New Jersey sells tax sale certificates, which are liens on the property, not the property itself. Each of the state's 566 municipalities must hold at least one tax sale a year, run by its own tax collector; many now hold them as online auctions, and some also hold an 'accelerated' sale late in the year for current-year charges unpaid after November 10. Certificates earn interest of up to 18 percent. Bidders compete by bidding the interest rate down and then by offering a premium, which the municipality holds on deposit for up to five years. If the owner does not redeem, the certificate holder can start foreclosure in Superior Court after two years.

overview_sources.quote: At the tax sale, title to the delinquent property itself is not sold. What is sold is a tax sale certificate, a lien on the property.
New Jersey law requires all 566 municipalities to hold at least one tax sale per year
Tax sale certificates can earn interest of up to 18 per cent, depending on the winning percentage bid at the auction.
The winning bidder is the one who bids the lowest percentage of interest or bids the highest premium.
After two years, a lien holder can begin proceedings in Superior Court to foreclose on the property.
